No civil registration of vital events existed in Norway until 1876 (national statistics level) or 1915 (community Folkeregistre). All births, marriages, and deaths in 1760-1821 were recorded only by the Lutheran Church in kirkebøker.

Women in this period used patronymic surnames, not their husband's surname. Unna Halsteinsdatter retained 'Halsteinsdatter' after marriage — she would not appear as 'Unna Monsen' in any 18th-century record. Search under 'Halsteinsdatter' (and variant spellings: Halsteindatter, Halsteinsdtr., Halst.dr.).
Church books from this period are written in Danish-influenced script (Kurrent/Gothic handwriting). Researchers must be able to read 18th-century Scandinavian handwriting or use a paleography guide.

The Norwegian patronymic naming pattern for this period: the first son was typically named for the father's father; the first daughter for the mother's mother. Knowledge of Unna's parents (Halstein + mother) and Anders's parents (Mons + mother) can guide searches for siblings and baptism records.

Some farms in Manger parish belonged to the Lysekloster Estate; probate records for those farms were kept at Hardanger og Voss rather than Nordhordaland Sorenskriveri — check both if probate searches in Nordhordaland come up empty.

The 1801 census is fully indexed at both FamilySearch (collection 3733603) and Digitalarkivet and names all household members. Since Anders died in 1821, the 1801 census may document him, Unna, and their children — use it to reconstruct the family even if the marriage record is not yet found.

The FamilySearch wiki page for Hamre prestegjeld genealogy returned no page during this survey (404); the Digitalarkivet browse interface for Hordaland (https://media.digitalarkivet.no/en/kb/browse?counties%5B%5D=12) is the primary route to Hamre church books.

# Locality Guide: Hordaland, Norway — Hamre and Manger Prestegjeld (1760–1821)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Civil county:** Bergenhus amt until 1763; **Søndre Bergenhus amt** 1763–1918; renamed Hordaland fylke 1919
- **Ecclesiastical:** Bergen (Bjørgvin) Diocese throughout; Nordhordaland Prosti (deanery)
- **County seat / administrative center:** Bergen
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Norway (Danish-Norwegian Crown union until 1814; Swedish union 1814–1905)
- **Population during period:** Hordaland province ~78,600–78,900 c. 1801 (estimate, Populstat); ~66,100 c. 1815 (estimate, reflecting Napoleonic-era disruption)
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, coastal fishing, some trade through Bergen
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly ethnic Norwegian; Bergen was a Hanseatic trade hub but the rural Nordhordaland parishes were nearly entirely Norwegian
- **Religious denominations:** Lutheran Church of Norway (state church) exclusively for this period; Dissenter Acts had not yet created significant non-Lutheran communities
- **Key historical events:** Napoleonic Wars (1807–1814) caused food shortages and reduced population; Norwegian constitution adopted 1814; union with Sweden 1814

## Boundary changes
- The civil amt was **Bergenhus** until 1763, then **Søndre Bergenhus** from 1763. Probate, tax, and land records filed before 1763 are indexed under Bergenhus.
- **Meland** was a chapel/annex within **Hamre prestegjeld** throughout the target period. Hamre prestegjeld also included the parishes of Åsane, Hamre (Hammer), and Alversund. There was no standalone Meland clerical district in 1760–1821; all church-book entries for Meland events appear in the Hamre prestegjeld registers.
- **Manger prestegjeld** is the adjacent clerical district to the south/west, covering Manger, Hordabø (Bøe), Sæbø, Herdla, and Hjelme. The Manger archive burned in 1759; surviving Manger records begin that year.
- **Hosanger prestegjeld** was separated from Hamre in 1749; earlier Hosanger records are in Hamre books.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Civil registration did not begin in Norway until 1876 (national statistical level) and community-level Folkeregistre began in 1915. The Norway Vital Records wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norway_Vital_Records) states: "No civil registration occurred in Norway until 1876." For 1760–1821, all vital event recording was by the Lutheran Church only.
- **Pre-1876 source:** Church books (kirkebøker) at parish level — see Church Records below.
- **Gaps:** No civil records exist for this period.

### Church records
- **Denomination:** Lutheran Church of Norway (sole state church); church books are the only vital records for this period.
- **Record types in kirkebøker:** Baptisms (christenings), confirmations, banns and marriages, burials, and in some registers: communion lists (communicants), household examination lists (husfoldsregister), and notes on illegitimate births.
- **Hamre prestegjeld (covers Meland in target period):**
  - The FamilySearch wiki page for Hamre prestegjeld genealogy was not available during this survey (404). Access Hamre records through the Digitalarkivet Hordaland church book browser: https://media.digitalarkivet.no/en/kb/browse?counties%5B%5D=12
  - FamilySearch Catalog: search for "Hamre prestegjeld" at https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog
- **Manger prestegjeld (adjacent; may hold records if family crossed parish lines):**
  - Archive burned 1759; all surviving records begin 1759.
  - 4 browse-only volumes on FamilySearch covering Manger Kyrkje 1759–1823 (imageGroupNumbers 008679417_001 through 008679417_004)
  - Digitalarkivet: Manger Parish Church Records 1759–1938 at https://media.digitalarkivet.no/kb/browse?archives%5B%5D=no-a1450-07000000001194
  - FamilySearch Catalog: Kirkebøker 1759–1923, Manger prestegjeld (catalog ID 58465)
- **Indexed collections covering this period:**
  - Norway, Marriages, 1660–1926 (FamilySearch collection 1468080, ~1.3M records, index only) — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1468080
  - Norway, Baptisms, 1634–1927 (FamilySearch collection 1467014, ~5.2M records, index only)
  - Norway, Burials, 1666–1927 (FamilySearch collection 1468081, ~716K records, index only)
  - Norway, Church Books, 1797–1958 (FamilySearch collection 4237104, ~14.4M records, 1.28M images) — covers the tail of the target period from 1797 onward
- **Language:** Records written in Danish (the administrative and ecclesiastical language of Norway through 1814); Norwegian forms increasingly appear after 1814. Old Kurrent/Gothic script — requires paleography skills.
- **Digitization level:** For Manger prestegjeld volumes found in volume_search: browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). The indexed FamilySearch collections (1468080, 1467014, 1468081) provide name-level searching but are index-only with no linked images.

### Census records
- **1801 national census:** Fully indexed at FamilySearch (collection 3733603, 878,979 records with images) and Digitalarkivet (https://www.digitalarkivet.no/en/census/search/1801). This is the only name-indexed nominative census in the target period. Anders Monsen (born 1759, died 1821) would have been approximately 42 years old in 1801; Unna Halsteinsdatter (born 1745) approximately 56.
- **Earlier male-only enumerations:** 1664–1666 and 1701 manntall (lists males only); both are images available at Digitalarkivet and on FamilySearch Catalog (koha:400373, koha:394978 include Manger).
- **1815–1855 partial counts:** Nominative lists of varying quality exist for some parishes; an overview is in Anna Tranberg, *Folk og Fant* (1986). None are fully indexed.
- **1825 census:** The FamilySearch Catalog has "1825 folketelling for Manger prestegjeld (Hordaland)" (koha:658668, microfilm 1283409) at the FamilySearch Library; also on Digitalarkivet. Similarly, "1835 folketelling for Hamre prestegjeld (Hordaland)" (koha:701507, film 1694692) exists and covers Meland.
- **Access:** 1801 census is indexed + images (free at FamilySearch); 1825 and 1835 local censuses are browse-only images at FamilySearch Center or Digitalarkivet.

### Probate and court records
- **Probate jurisdiction:** Nordhordaland Sorenskriveri (district court/probate) covers Manger and Hamre prestegjeld.
- **Types:** Skifteprotokoller (probate registers recording estate divisions after death) — these list heirs by name and relationship, making them valuable for identifying spouses and children.
- **Date range and access:**
  - Skifteprotokoller 1702–1910, Nordhordaland Sorenskriveri — FamilySearch Catalog (koha:438738), images
  - Skifteprotokoller 1773–1810, Nordhordland Prosti — FamilySearch Catalog (koha:438920), images
  - Norway, Probate Index Cards, 1640–1903 (FamilySearch collection 1661306, ~1M records, indexed) — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1661306
  - Scanned probate records at Digitalarkivet: https://media.digitalarkivet.no/en/sk/browse
- **Note:** Some farms in Manger parish belonged to the Lysekloster Estate; their probate records are filed at Hardanger og Voss (not Nordhordaland) — search both if needed.
- **Court records:** Tingbøker 1642–1701, Nordhordaland Sorenskriveri, on FamilySearch Catalog (koha with film 505971). These record local court proceedings that may name individuals not in other sources.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds; property identified by farm name (*gård*) and farm number (*bruksnummer*)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Norwegian Crown (via local lensmenn and fogder); original land grants are in Rentekammeret records
- **Types:** Pantebøker (mortgage/deed registers), matrikkelen (land register), tax lists
- **Date range and access:**
  - Pantebøker 1741–1893, Nordhordaland — FamilySearch Catalog (koha:494924), images
  - Matrikkelen 1661, 1665, 1723 for Hordaland — FamilySearch Catalog (koha:651320), images
  - Lensregnskaper 1563–1661 (estate/tax accounts) — FamilySearch Catalog (koha:501015)
  - Norway Property Records at Digitalarkivet: https://www.digitalarkivet.no/content/111/eiendom-og-tinglysing
  - Taxation and accounting records: https://www.digitalarkivet.no/content/85/regnskap-og-skatt

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Great Northern War aftermath; Napoleonic Wars (1807–1814) when Norway was under Danish rule
- **Record types:** Militærrulles (muster rolls); Bergenhusiske infanteriregiment records
- **Date range and access:**
  - Militærrulle 1658 for Nordhordlandske kompani at Digitalarkivet (source 100157)
  - Militærrulle 1714 and 1722 at Digitalarkivet (sources 100454, 100456)
  - Norway Military Records guide: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norway_Military_Records
- **Coverage gap:** Comprehensive muster rolls for 1760–1821 are not detailed in the sources returned by this survey; consult Statsarkivet i Bergen directly for 18th-century military records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Parish churchyards (kirkegård) at each parish church; Meland Kyrkegard, Manger churchyard
- **Online coverage:** BillionGraves at https://billiongraves.com/site-map?country=Norway; FindAGrave Norway page at https://www.findagrave.com/cemetery/search?cemetery-name=&cemetery-loc=Norway; DIS-Norge Burial Index (1700–2010) at https://slektogdata.no/gravminner (index only); Nettgrav at https://nettgrav.no/finn-en-grav
- **Physical records:** Sexton (gravedigger) registers and church burial books — part of the kirkebøker series; subject to same browse-only limitations

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Bergen-based newspapers existed in this period (Bergens Adressecontoirs Efterretninger, founded 1763) but rural Nordhordaland parishes would have minimal coverage
- **Online:** Norway Newspapers at National Library (https://www.nb.no/search?mediatype=aviser); MyHeritage Norway Newspapers collection
- **Content value for this period:** Very limited for rural families; legal notices and property transfers occasionally name rural persons

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant period:** Mass emigration from Norway did not begin until the 1830s–1840s. For 1760–1821, emigration was negligible.
- **Record types (post-period context):** Emigration passports from Bergen 1842–1860 at Digitalarkivet (source 100013); Bergen ship lists 1865–1873 (source 100097)
- **Naturalizations:** Not applicable for this period
- **Inland records:** Husfoldsregistre (household examination lists) in church books note when families moved between parishes — useful for tracking migration within Norway

### Tax records
- **Types:** Lensregnskaper (estate/bailiff accounts), fogderiregnskaper (tax collector accounts), extra taxes (e.g., 1762–1772 Extra tax)
- **Date range:** Lensregnskaper 1563–1661 on FamilySearch Catalog; Regnskaper 1661–1692, Stiftamtstue Bergenhus on FamilySearch Catalog (koha:498484)
- **Oppebørselbok for Rosendalsgodset 1796–1800 at Digitalarkivet (source 100486)** — covers some Hordaland estates
- **Online:** Norway Accounting and Tax Records at https://www.digitalarkivet.no/content/85/regnskap-og-skatt
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists supplement censuses in years with no nominative count

### Other record types
- **Bygdebøker (farm/village books):** Compiled local histories that often reconstruct family genealogies from church books. Several Hordaland parish bygdebøker exist; the FamilySearch Library holds multiple volumes (e.g., *Radøy gjennom tidene*, which covers Manger-area farms). A list of digitized bygdebøker is at https://martinroe.com/blog/bygdeboker-available-online/
- **Husfoldsregistre (household examination lists):** Maintained by pastors and recording all parishioners' communion attendance and literacy; sometimes names household members not otherwise visible. These appear within the kirkebøker series.
- **Court (Ting) records:** Tingbøker record local affairs including land disputes, social welfare, and road maintenance — naming individuals not in vital or census records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Norway Marriages 1660–1926 (col. 1468080); Norway Baptisms 1634–1927 (col. 1467014); Norway Burials 1666–1927 (col. 1468081); Norway Census 1801 (col. 3733603); Norway Church Books 1797–1958 (col. 4237104); Norway Probate Index Cards 1640–1903 (col. 1661306) | Free |
| Digitalarkivet | All Hordaland church books (images); 1801 census index+images; probate records; land/property records; tax records; emigration | Free — https://digitalarkivet.no/ |
| Ancestry | Norway Marriages 1600s–1800s; Norway Births & Christenings 1648–1903; Norway Select Baptisms 1634–1927; 1801 Census | Subscription — https://www.ancestry.com |
| MyHeritage | Norway Church Records 1815–1938; Norway Baptisms 1634–1927; Norway Marriages 1660–1926; 1801 Census | Subscription — https://www.myheritage.com |
| FindMyPast | Norway Baptisms 1634–1927; Norway Burials 1666–1927; Norway Marriage Index 1660–1926 | Subscription — https://www.findmypast.com |

**Digitalarkivet church book browser for Hordaland:** https://media.digitalarkivet.no/en/kb/browse?counties%5B%5D=12 — this is the primary image access point for Hamre and Manger prestegjeld registers.

**Coverage of this survey:** 62 digitized volumes match Hordaland 1760–1821 in FamilySearch's volume system; the first 50 were examined in detail above. The volume_search summary (complete) shows all 62: 34 religious/church record volumes (all browse-only), 4 baptism volumes (all browse-only), 2 religious marriage volumes (browse-only), 23 census volumes (indexed for 1801), plus legal, government, and vital record volumes. No volumes are full-text searchable.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Statsarkivet i Bergen (Regional State Archives) | Original kirkebøker for all Hordaland parishes; probate; land; military for this period | In-person or digital request — https://www.arkivverket.no |
| National Archives of Norway (Riksarkivet), Oslo | Central government records; Rentekammeret (tax/land); military central records | In-person or online — https://www.riksarkivet.no |
| FamilySearch Library, Salt Lake City | Microfilm of most Hordaland kirkebøker; probate; censuses | Free in-person; some catalog items viewable at FamilySearch Centers |

## Records NOT online
- **Hamre prestegjeld church books (pre-1797):** The FamilySearch-indexed Church Books collection begins in 1797. Hamre prestegjeld church books for 1760–1796 may only be accessible as browse-only images at Digitalarkivet (https://media.digitalarkivet.no/en/kb/browse?counties%5B%5D=12) or as microfilm at the FamilySearch Library. The FamilySearch wiki page for Hamre prestegjeld was unavailable during this survey; browse Digitalarkivet directly.
- **Husfoldsregistre (household examination lists):** Rarely name-indexed; must be browsed page by page within the kirkebøker volumes.
- **Tingbøker (court minute books) for Nordhordaland post-1701:** The FamilySearch Catalog entry (film 505971) covers 1642–1701; later court books may require a request to Statsarkivet i Bergen.
- **Military muster rolls 1760–1821:** Detailed muster rolls for this period are not in the indexed collections found during this survey.

## Known record losses
- **Manger prestegjeld archive fire, 1759:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Manger_Parish,_Hordaland,_Norway_Genealogy): "The Archive burned in 1759." All Manger parish records before that year are destroyed. Substitute: earlier 1664–1666 and 1701 male manntall may document ancestors, but baptism and marriage records before 1759 for Manger are lost.
- No other specific record losses for Hamre prestegjeld were reported in the sources retrieved during this survey. Empty search results in a collection are a coverage gap, not confirmed destruction.

## Research tips
- **Start with the indexed marriage collection.** Search Norway, Marriages, 1660–1926 (FamilySearch collection 1468080, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1468080) for Anders Monsen and Unna Halsteinsdatter. This index draws from church book extracts; a hit will give a parish and date to then verify in the original image.
- **Search all name variants.** Per the Norway Naming Customs wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norway_Naming_Customs), spelling was not standardized until 1917 and names were frequently abbreviated. Try: Unna/Una/Unne; Halsteinsdatter/Halsteindatter/Halsteinsdtr./Halst.dr.; Monsen/Munsen; Anders/Andres.
- **Women retained their patronymic name.** Per the Norway Naming Customs wiki: patronymic surnames were the norm and women did not take their husband's surname in this period. Unna Halsteinsdatter would appear in every record as Halsteinsdatter — never as Unna Monsen.
- **Use the 1801 census to anchor the family.** The 1801 census (FamilySearch collection 3733603, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/3733603) is fully indexed and names all household members with ages and relationships. Anders (b. 1759) and Unna (b. 1745) would both be listed if living; their children's names and approximate birth years will appear.
- **Browse Hamre prestegjeld church books directly at Digitalarkivet** (https://media.digitalarkivet.no/en/kb/browse?counties%5B%5D=12). ## Marriage of Anders Monsen and Unna Halsteinsdatter

Anders Monsen and Unna Halsteinsdatter were married on **25 June 1786** at **Hamre, Hordaland, Norway**. Two independent sources establish this conclusion: the 1786 church marriage register and the 1801 Norwegian census.

### Marriage Register

"Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926," *FamilySearch* (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:NW44-PM2 : Thu Oct 08 17:58:07 UTC 2026), Entry for Anders Monsen and Urna Halsteinsdr, 25 June 1786 [hereafter Marriage Register]. The Marriage Register records Anders Monsen as groom and "Urna Halsteinsdr" as bride for a marriage solemnized on 25 June 1786 at Hamre, Hordaland, Norway.

This entry is an original record of the event: the officiating Lutheran pastor recorded the marriage contemporaneously in the Hamre prestegjeld church register, with both parties present as informants. The information quality is therefore primary, and the record basis is stated. Civil registration of vital events did not begin in Norway until the mid-to-late nineteenth century; the Lutheran church register is the sole authoritative record type for an 1786 marriage in Hordaland, and no alternative source could independently record the date and place.

"Urna Halsteinsdr" is an expected eighteenth-century Norwegian scribal variant for "Unna Halsteinsdatter." Norwegian spelling was not standardized until 1917; the given-name alternation "Urna/Unna" and the surname abbreviation "Halsteinsdr" for "Halsteinsdatter" are well-documented conventions of the period and do not undermine identification. The groom "Anders Monsen" is identified as tree person LKFW-9XH: the name matches exactly, the location (Hamre, Hordaland) is consistent with LKFW-9XH's recorded Hordaland birthplace, and the bride is recorded as LKFW-9XH's known spouse (person-evidence match score 0.974). The bride "Urna Halsteinsdr" is identified as tree person KZHH-VTX: the name variant is recognized, and the co-groom "Anders Monsen" matches KZHH-VTX's known spouse (match score 0.904). The co-identification is mutually reinforcing.

### 1801 Census Corroboration

"Norges folketelling, 1801," *FamilySearch* (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:8YMK-6G3Z : Sun Oct 12 18:32:55 UTC 2025), Entry for Ingebor Nielsdatter and Anders Monsen, 1801 [hereafter 1801 Census]. The 1801 Census records "Anders Monsen" (age 45) and "Udna Halstensdatter" (age 56) living together at Åsebø farm (Aasebø), Manger, Hordaland — fifteen years after the marriage. The census was compiled by an enumerator who visited the dwelling; the household informant is unknown, so information quality is indeterminate. The census does not independently record the marriage date or place.

The 1801 Census corroborates both parties' identities: "Udna Halstensdatter" is a recognized Norwegian spelling variant of "Unna Halsteinsdatter," and Udna's age of 56 implies birth about 1745 — matching KZHH-VTX's recorded birth date of May 1745 (match score 0.815). The child Jørgen Andersen (age 5, born about 1796) also appears in the household; the patronymic "Andersen" (son of Anders in Norwegian naming convention) is consistent with Anders Monsen as his father.

Anders's reported age of 45 in 1801 implies birth about 1756, three years earlier than his tree-recorded birth date of 7 April 1759. This three-year gap is within the normal range of census approximation for Norwegian eighteenth-century enumerations and does not create a factual conflict. The marriage register carries no birth date for Anders, so no discrepancy exists within the marriage evidence itself.

guardrail_shadow_violations.detail: person_evidence link written for new tree person(s) I1, I2 with no prior same_person call: a brand-new identity should be scored before it is asserted (person-evidence/SKILL.md doctrine; issue #963). Score them with the project-relative form, which assembles both documents for you: `same_person({ projectPath, assertionId, treePersonId: "I1" })`. `assertionId` is the assertion the link cites. The tool resolves the record itself and builds the tree side as that person's matching mob, so you hand-build nothing (person-evidence, 'Call it with references, not documents'). If this call was denied, the entire batch was rejected — including any ops in other sections — and must be re-issued after the same_person call. A relationship or marriage assertion names two parties and gets a link for each. The call is about the assertion's own `record_role` party by default; for the OTHER party add `recordRole` (or `recordPersonaId`) naming it. Reusing the first party's persona for the second is how a near-zero score gets manufactured and then explained away. If the tool answers that the record holds no persona for that party, or that the candidate is a stub minted from the very persona you would be scoring (circular), say so in the link's `rationale` and proceed — the gap is still recorded; the rationale is the record of why, not a waiver. How the assertion was RETRIEVED is not such a case: a full-text hit, an image, a PDF and a sidecar-less search are all scorable, because the tool derives the record side from the record's own assertions when it cannot fetch a document. A locally-minted tree id is NOT such a case: it scores on document content and must be scored.
